title: Memory variants and what they mean for test
summary: Besides the plain single-port SRAM, a chip contains multi-port memories, ROMs and — in FPGAs — block RAM and distributed (LUT) RAM. Each one changes **how the BIST must test it**. DRAM and flash are mentioned briefly; the details of all memories belong to the Digital Design courses.
objectives: Explain what extra testing a multi-port memory needs.
Explain how a ROM is tested without writing.
Explain synchronous and asynchronous read and why the MBIST comparator must know the read latency.
Name the special concerns of DRAM and flash tests.

blocks.alt: Dual-port memory with port A and port B around a shared cell array
blocks.caption: Dual-port memory

blocks.md:
A **dual-port** memory has two complete sets of address, data and control signals. Both ports can read or write **at the same time**, even the same cell. Processor **register files** go further: typically two read ports and one write port per clock.

Every cell gets extra access transistors and bit lines for each port — and with them, new ways to fail.

rows: Run the single-port test **through every port**
a port's own decoder, bit lines or sense amplifiers can be broken while the other port works
Add **inter-port** tests: both ports active in the same clock
a short between the bit lines of two ports, or a weak cell that fails only when both ports load it
what the memory does when both ports write the same address is defined by the memory — the test must not expect anything else
blocks.caption: Testing multi-port memories

blocks.md: A **ROM** is written once, when the chip is made. A test that writes data is impossible, so the BIST simply **reads every word** and compacts the data in a **MISR** — exactly the response compaction of *BIST Foundations*, Topic 5.

blocks.alt: Address counter drives the ROM, the ROM data goes into a MISR, the signature is compared
blocks.caption: ROM BIST = address counter + MISR

blocks.title: Where the golden signature comes from
blocks.md: The ROM content is a file (the boot code image). The design flow computes the expected signature from that file. If the ROM content changes, the golden signature must change with it — usually generated automatically.

subsections.title: FPGA memories: block RAM and LUT RAM

blocks.md: FPGAs offer two kinds of on-chip RAM, and an MBIST built into an FPGA design has to handle both:

tabs.label: Block RAM (BRAM)
tabs.md: Dedicated memory blocks of a fixed size (for example 36 Kb blocks in AMD devices, 20 Kb M20K blocks in Intel devices), configurable in width and depth, single- or dual-port. **Synchronous read**: the address is taken at a clock edge and the data appears **after** that edge — one clock later, or two with the optional output register.

tabs.label: LUT RAM (distributed RAM)
tabs.md: Small memories built from the look-up tables of the logic blocks (AMD: distributed RAM; Intel: MLAB). Writes are synchronous, but the **read is asynchronous**: the data follows the address within the same clock cycle, like combinational logic.

blocks.alt: Timing: LUTRAM data appears in the same cycle, BRAM data one clock later
blocks.caption: Read latency: 0 clocks (LUTRAM) or 1 clock (BRAM)

blocks.title: Why the MBIST must know the latency
blocks.md: The MBIST comparator checks the read data against the **expected** value. With a BRAM, the data of the read issued in clock *n* arrives in clock *n + 1* — so the expected value (and the address, for the fail log) must be **delayed by the same latency**. A wrong latency makes a perfect memory look broken, or hides real failures.

blocks.caption: 1T1C DRAM cell: the bit is a charge on a capacitor

blocks.md:
A DRAM cell stores a bit as **charge on a tiny capacitor**, behind one access transistor — far smaller than a 6T SRAM cell. The charge **leaks**, so every row is refreshed regularly, and a read **destroys** the value, so it is written back after every read.

The key DRAM tests are **retention** (does a cell keep its charge long enough between refreshes, also when hot?) and **disturb** effects between neighbouring rows. DRAM is usually a separate chip tested by its maker; an SoC's memory controller may also run a memory test at boot.

tabs.label: Flash
tabs.md: Non-volatile cells that are **programmed** and **erased** in blocks, slowly, and wear out after many cycles. Tests check program/erase, **endurance** and read margins. Embedded flash in microcontrollers has its own built-in test modes.

blocks.title: Focus of this course
blocks.md: From here on we concentrate on **SRAM** — the memories that MBIST tests in almost every chip, including the block RAM and LUT RAM of FPGAs.

questions.text: What does an MBIST need for a dual-port memory? Select **all** correct answers.
options: Run the memory test through each port.
Test both ports active in the same clock.
Respect the memory's rule for two writes to the same address.
Test only port A — port B uses the same cells.

questions.text: How is a ROM tested by BIST?
options: Read every word and compact the data in a MISR; compare with the signature computed from the ROM file.
Run a March test that writes 0s and 1s.
Compare it with a second ROM on the chip.
ROMs cannot have defects, so they are not tested.

questions.text: In an FPGA, which memory has an **asynchronous** read (data in the same clock cycle)?
options: LUT RAM (distributed RAM)
Block RAM
Both
Neither

questions.text: An MBIST tests a BRAM with one clock of read latency but compares the data in the same clock as the read. What happens?
options: The comparison uses the wrong data: good memories fail or real faults are missed.
Nothing — the BRAM adapts its latency.
The test only runs slower.
Only the first address is affected.

questions.text: Why must a DRAM be refreshed?
options: The charge on its capacitors leaks away.
Its sense amplifiers forget the data.
Its address decoder needs a periodic reset.
SRAM needs refresh too, DRAM does not.
